scope: AQA 7405 3.1.1.1, 3.1.1.2, 3.1.1.3: fundamental particles; mass number/isotopes/simple TOF; electron configurations and successive ionisation energy
auditLevel: Front/back first-pass plausibility and scope review of 88 AS core cards from three exact topic labels, plus explicit 29-point requirement-to-card evidence mapping. Not an examiner verification of every alternative or unfamiliar numerical application.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Define relative atomic mass, Ar.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Weighted mean mass of an atom relative to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What are isotopes?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Define first ionisation energy.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form gaseous 1+ ions.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why generally does first ionisation energy increase across a period?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Nuclear charge increases while shielding is similar, so attraction to the outer electron increases and atomic radius falls.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the difference between atomic number and mass number?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Atomic number is number of protons; mass number is protons plus neutrons.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: State the relative charge and mass of a proton.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Charge +1, relative mass 1.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: State the relative charge and mass of a neutron.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Charge 0, relative mass 1.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: State the relative charge and mass of an electron.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Charge −1, relative mass about 1/1836.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What does the proton number Z measure?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: The number of protons in a nucleus; it defines the element.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: How are neutrons counted using A and Z?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Number of neutrons = mass number A − proton number Z.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: How many electrons are in a 3+ ion formed from Z=13?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: 13−3 = 10 electrons; the nucleus is unchanged.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why did Rutherford reject the plum pudding model?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Some alpha particles scattered through large angles, implying a tiny, dense positive nucleus.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why do isotopes often have similar chemical properties?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: They have the same electron arrangements despite differing neutron numbers.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Define relative molecular mass Mr.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Mean mass of a molecule compared with 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is relative isotopic mass compared against?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: One twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: How do you calculate Ar from two isotope abundances?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: (isotope mass₁×abundance₁ + mass₂×abundance₂) ÷ total abundance.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is Ar of an isotope mixture a weighted mean?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: More abundant isotopes contribute more to the average mass.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What does m/z mean in mass spectrometry?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Mass-to-charge ratio; for a singly charged ion it matches the relative ion mass.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What are the four core TOF stages in order?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Ionisation → acceleration → ion drift → detection/data analysis.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the purpose of ionisation in TOF?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: To give sample particles an electrical charge so they can be accelerated and detected.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is formed by electron-impact ionisation of X(g)?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: X⁺(g), after an electron is removed.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why may electron-impact mass spectra show fragment peaks?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Energetic ionisation can break molecules into smaller charged fragments.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What charge is commonly formed by electrospray protonation?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: A singly charged protonated ion, [M+H]⁺.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why can electrospray help analyse large molecules?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: It is gentler and often causes less fragmentation than electron impact.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What happens to positive ions in the acceleration stage?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: An electric field accelerates them, giving ions of equal charge equal kinetic energy.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why does equal kinetic energy not mean equal speed?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Since Eₖ=½mv², lighter ions have greater speed at equal Eₖ.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Which travels faster at equal KE: 63⁺ or 65⁺?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: The lighter 63⁺ ion.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the purpose of the flight/drift tube?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: To time how long accelerated ions take to travel a fixed distance.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is a high vacuum used in the drift tube?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: To reduce collisions between moving ions and gas molecules.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What happens to an ion's speed while drifting ideally?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: It remains approximately constant in the field-free drift region.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the relationship between flight time, distance and speed?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Flight time t = flight length L ÷ speed v.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: How does flight time change as mass increases at fixed KE and charge?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: It increases; t is proportional to the square root of mass.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What happens when ions reach a TOF detector?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: They generate an electrical signal used to record ion arrivals.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What does the position of a mass spectrum peak indicate?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Its mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What does the height/intensity of a mass spectrum peak indicate?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Relative abundance of the detected ion.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the base peak in a mass spectrum?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: The most intense peak; it is assigned 100% relative intensity.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is the base peak not necessarily the molecular ion?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: A charged fragment can be more abundant than the intact molecular ion.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What does a molecular-ion peak represent in electron-impact MS?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: An ion formed from the intact molecule after losing an electron.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why might the electrospray [M+H]⁺ peak differ from molecular mass?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: It includes the mass of an added proton; m/z is about Mr+1 for 1+ ions.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: For a 36 u ion with a 2+ charge, what is m/z?
At fixed voltage, how does a higher ion charge affect kinetic energy?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Eₖ=qV; a higher charge gains more kinetic energy.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What simple relation links acceleration voltage and ion energy?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Kinetic energy gained = charge × potential difference, Eₖ=qV.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: How can elemental identity be suggested by mass spectrometry?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Compare isotope peak masses and relative abundances to characteristic isotope patterns.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Write the first ionisation equation for magnesium.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Write the second ionisation equation for magnesium.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why do successive ionisation energies increase?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What does a very large successive-IE jump identify?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Removal has reached an inner shell; the number removed before it equals outer-shell electrons.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why does first IE usually rise across Period 3?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Nuclear charge rises; shielding changes little; outer electrons are held more strongly.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is Al first IE lower than Mg first IE?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Al loses a higher-energy 3p electron; Mg loses a lower-energy 3s electron.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is S first IE lower than P first IE?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Electron repulsion within a paired 3p orbital in S helps one electron escape.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why does first IE fall down Group 2?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Outer electrons are farther away and more shielded, despite a larger nuclear charge.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: How many electrons can an s, p and d subshell hold?
What are the exceptional electron configurations of chromium and copper?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹; Cu: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the configuration of Fe²⁺?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: [Ar]3d⁶; electrons are removed from 4s before 3d.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the configuration of Fe³⁺?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: [Ar]3d⁵; after both 4s electrons, one 3d electron is lost.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is Hund's rule when filling degenerate orbitals?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly before pairing.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Write chromium's ground-state electron configuration.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Write copper's ground-state electron configuration.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why does Cr have one 4s electron rather than two?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Its 3d⁵ half-filled subshell is especially favourable.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why does Cu have one 4s electron rather than two?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Its 3d¹⁰ full subshell is especially favourable.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Which element has a half-filled 3d subshell: Cr or Cu?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Chromium (Cr).

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the electron configuration of Cr³⁺?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: [Ar]3d³. Remove the 4s electron first, then two 3d electrons.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the electron configuration of Cu²⁺?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: [Ar]3d⁹. Remove one 4s electron and then one 3d electron.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the electron configuration of Cu⁺?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: [Ar]3d¹⁰. Remove copper's 4s¹ electron.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: When transition-metal ions form, which electrons leave first?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: The 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is '4s fills first, so 3d empties first' incorrect?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: 4s generally fills before 3d, but 4s electrons are removed first in these ions.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: How does shielding change across Period 3, helping first ionisation energy rise?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: It remains approximately the same.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Which two different causes explain the Period 3 first-IE dips?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Mg→Al: higher-energy 3p versus 3s. P→S: extra repulsion from paired 3p electrons.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Which two drops interrupt the general rise in first ionisation energy across Period 3?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Mg to Al (3p electron) and P to S (3p electron pairing).

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is the relative isotopic mass?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Isotope mass relative to 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why are successive ionisation energies always positive?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Removing an electron requires energy to overcome attraction.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What causes a large jump between successive ionisation energies?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: The next electron is removed from an inner shell.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is 4s filled before 3d?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: 4s is initially lower in energy in neutral atoms.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why are 4s electrons removed before 3d electrons from transition-metal ions?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: The 4s electrons become higher in energy in these ions.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What is meant by an isotope?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What does the molecular-ion peak show in a mass spectrum?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: The relative molecular mass of the molecular ion.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why do ions of different mass take different flight times in a TOF mass spectrometer?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: At the same kinetic energy, lighter ions travel faster.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What causes ions to produce a signal at the TOF detector?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Ion impacts produce an electrical signal.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: How is the weighted mean relative atomic mass calculated?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Sum of (isotopic mass × abundance) divided by total abundance.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What change occurs to electron configuration when forming a cation?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Electrons are removed from the outermost occupied shell first.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: For transition-metal cations, which sub-shell loses electrons before 3d?
Why is the first ionisation energy of sulfur below phosphorus?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Electron-pair repulsion in sulfur's 3p sub-shell.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is the first ionisation energy of aluminium below magnesium?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Aluminium loses a higher-energy 3p electron.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why is a big jump in successive ionisation energies significant?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: It indicates removal from a new, inner electron shell.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Fill the gap: successive ionisation energies show electron ____.
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: shell structure.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Why are time-of-flight mass-spectrometer ions given the same kinetic energy?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: So flight time depends on mass-to-charge ratio.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: Which ions arrive sooner in a TOF tube at equal kinetic energy: lower or higher m/z?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: Lower m/z ions.

coreCardsFirstPass.originalFront: What does a mass spectrum's relative abundance quantify?
coreCardsFirstPass.originalBack: The proportion of detected ions giving a peak.
